        unit_id: p000023
        locator: Page 23, characters 0–2523
        available_excerpt: "23 \n \nprocess: \n(1) \nthe [Commissioner] is authorized
          and encouraged to accept the \ninvestigation results of a lead investigative
          state for the purpose of [Section 6.01(g)] if the \nlead investigative state
          has sufficient staffing, expertise, and minimum standards; or \n(2) \nif
          [state] is a lead investigative state, the [Commissioner] is \nauthorized
          and encouraged to investigate the applicant pursuant to [Section 6.01(g)]
          and \nthe timeframes established by agreement through the multistate licensing
          process. \n(i) \nThe [Commissioner] shall issue a formal written notice
          of the denial of an \napplication to acquire control within thirty (30)
          days of the decision to deny the application. The \n[Commissioner] shall
          set forth in the notice of denial the specific reasons for the denial of
          the \napplication. An applicant whose application is denied by the [Commissioner]
          under this [Section \n6.01(i)] may appeal within thirty (30) days16 after
          receipt of the written notice of the denial \n[pursuant to state administrative
          law procedures]. \n(j) \nThe requirements of [Section 6.01(a) and (b)] do
          not apply to any of the \nfollowing: \n(1) \nA person that acts as a proxy
          for the sole purpose of voting at a \ndesignated meeting of the shareholders
          or holders of voting shares or voting interests of a \nlicensee or a person
          in control of a licensee; \n(2) \nA person that acquires control of a licensee
          by devise or descent; \n(3) \nA person that acquires control of a licensee
          as a personal \nrepresentative, custodian, guardian, conservator, or trustee,
          or as an officer appointed by a \ncourt of competent jurisdiction or by
          operation of law; \n(4) \nA person that is exempt under [Section 3.01(g)];
          \n(5) \nA person that the [Commissioner] determines is not subject to \n[Section
          6.01(a)] based on the public interest; \n(6) \nA public offering of securities
          of a licensee or a person in control of \na licensee; or \n(7) \nAn internal
          reorganization of a person in control of the licensee \nwhere the ultimate
          person in control of the licensee remains the same. \n(k) \nPersons in [Sections
          6.01(j)(2), (3), (4), (6), (7)] in cooperation with the \nlicensee shall
          notify the [Commissioner] within [15] days after the acquisition of control.17
          \n \n16 Commentary: Administrative procedures for challenging a departmental
          decision may be derived from other \naspects of state law. In such a case,
          this Act should be adjusted to reflect the relevant administrative process.
          \n17 Commentary: Notice is satisfied upon updating the licensee’s NMLS record.\n"

        unit_id: p000024
        locator: Page 24, characters 0–2799
        available_excerpt: "24 \n \n(l) \nStreamlined Acquisition of Control \n(1)
          \nThe requirements of [Section 6.01(a) and (b)] do not apply to a \nperson
          that has complied with and received approval to engage in money transmission
          \nunder this [Act] or was identified as a person in control in a prior application
          filed with and \napproved by the [Commissioner] or by an MSB accredited
          state pursuant to a multistate \nlicensing process, provided that: \n(A)
          \nthe person has not had a license revoked or suspended or \ncontrolled
          a licensee that has had a license revoked or suspended while the person
          \nwas in control of the licensee in the previous 5-years; \n(B) \nif the
          person is a licensee, the person is well managed and \nhas received at least
          a satisfactory rating for compliance at its most recent \nexamination by
          an MSB accredited state if such rating was given; \n(C) \nthe licensee to
          be acquired is projected to meet the \nrequirements of [Sections 10.01,
          10.02, and 10.03] of this [Act] after the acquisition \nof control is completed,
          and if the person acquiring control is a licensee, that \nlicensee is also
          projected to meet the requirements of [Sections 10.01, 10.02, and \n10.03]
          of this [Act] after the acquisition of control is completed; \n(D) \nthe
          licensee to be acquired will not implement any material \nchanges to its
          business plan as a result of the acquisition of control, and if the person
          \nacquiring control is a licensee, that licensee also will not implement
          any material \nchanges to its business plan as a result of the acquisition
          of control;  and \n(E) \nthe person provides notice of the acquisition in
          cooperation \nwith the licensee and attests to [Section 6.01(l)(1)(A), (B),
          (C), and (D)] in a form \nand in a medium prescribed by the [Commissioner].
          \n(2) \nIf the notice is not disapproved within 30 days after the date on
          \nwhich the notice was determined to be complete, the notice is deemed approved.
          \n(m) \nBefore filing an application for approval to acquire control of
          a licensee a \nperson may request in writing a determination from the [Commissioner]
          as to whether the person \nwould be considered a person in control of a
          licensee upon consummation of a proposed \ntransaction. If the [Commissioner]
          determines that the person would not be a person in control of \na licensee,
          the proposed Person and transaction is not subject to the requirements of
          [Section \n6.01(a) and (b)] of this [Act]. \n(n) \nIf a multistate licensing
          process includes a determination pursuant to \n[Section 6.01(m)] and an
          applicant avails itself or is otherwise subject to the multistate licensing
          \nprocess: \n(1) \nThe [Commissioner] is authorized and encouraged to accept
          the \ncontrol determination of a lead investigative state with sufficient
          staffing, expertise, and \nminimum standards for the purpose of [Section
          6.01(m)]; or\n"

        available_excerpt: "ly for goods or services provided by the issuer or its
          affiliate or franchisees of the issuer \nor its affiliate, except to the
          extent required by applicable law to be redeemable in cash for its cash
          \nvalue; \n(f) \n\"Control\" means \n(1) \n(A) the power to vote, directly
          or indirectly, at least 25 percent of \nthe outstanding voting shares or
          voting interests of a licensee or person in control of a \nlicensee; \n(B)
          \nthe power to elect or appoint a majority of key individuals or \nexecutive
          officers, managers, directors, trustees, or other persons exercising \nmanagerial
          authority of a person in control of a licensee; or \n(C) \nthe power to
          exercise, directly or indirectly, a controlling \ninfluence over the management
          or policies of a licensee or person in control of a \nlicensee. \n(2) \nRebuttable
          Presumption of Control. \n(A) \nA person is presumed to exercise a controlling
          influence \nwhen the person holds the power to vote, directly or indirectly,
          at least 10 percent \nof the outstanding voting shares or voting interests
          of a licensee or person in control \nof a licensee.2 \n(B) \nA person presumed
          to exercise a controlling influence as \ndefined by this [Section 2.01(f)]
          can rebut the presumption of control if the person \nis a passive investor.
          \n(3) \nFor purposes of determining the percentage of a person controlled
          \nby any other person, the person's interest shall be aggregated with the
          interest of any other \nimmediate family member, including the person's
          spouse, parents, children, siblings, \nmothers- and fathers-in law, sons-
          and daughters-in-law, brothers- and sisters-in-law, and \nany other person
          who shares such person's home. \n(g) \n\"Eligible rating\" shall mean a
          credit rating of any of the three highest rating \ncategories provided by
          an eligible rating service, whereby each category may include rating \n
          \n2 Commentary: The obligation to rebut control rests exclusively with the
          person acquiring ≥10% of the outstanding \nvoting shares or voting interests
          of a licensee or person in control of a licensee.  It is not the responsibility
          of the \nlicensee to rebut control.  This is consistent with Section 601(a)
          of the Act which requires the person acquiring control \nto obtain prior
          approval.\n"

        available_excerpt: "30 \n \n(1) \nappoint the person signing the contract

          transmission on behalf of the licensee; \n(2) \nset forth the nature and
          scope of the relationship between the \nlicensee and the authorized delegate
          and the respective rights and responsibilities of the \nparties; \n(3) \nrequire
          the authorized delegate to agree to fully comply with all \napplicable state
          and federal laws, rules, and regulations pertaining to money transmission,
          \nincluding this [Act] and regulations implementing this [Act], relevant
          provisions of the \nBank Secrecy Act and the USA PATRIOT ACT; \n(4) \nrequire
          the authorized delegate to remit and handle money and \nmonetary value in
          accordance with the terms of the contract between the licensee and the \nauthorized
          delegate; \n(5) \nimpose a trust on money and monetary value net of fees
          received for \nmoney transmission for the benefit of the licensee; \n(6)
          \nrequire the authorized delegate to prepare and maintain records as \nrequired
          by this [Act] or regulations implementing this [Act], or as reasonably requested
          \nby the [Commissioner]; \n(7) \nacknowledge that the authorized delegate
          consents to examination \nor investigation by the [Commissioner]; \n(8)
          \nstate that the licensee is subject to regulation by the [Commissioner]
          \nand that, as part of that regulation, the [Commissioner] may suspend or
          revoke an \nauthorized delegate designation or require the licensee to terminate
          an authorized delegate \ndesignation; and \n(9) \n(9)  acknowledge receipt
          of the written policies and procedures \nrequired under [Section 8.01(b)(1)].
          \n(e) \nIf the licensee's license is suspended, revoked, surrendered, or
          expired, the \nlicensee must, within five (5) business days, provide documentation
          to the [Commissioner] that \nthe licensee has notified all applicable authorized
          delegates of the licensee whose names are in a \nrecord filed with the [Commissioner]
          of the suspension, revocation, surrender, or expiration of a \nlicense.
          Upon suspension, revocation, surrender, or expiration of a license, applicable
          authorized \ndelegates shall immediately cease to provide money transmission
          as an authorized delegate of the \nlicensee. \n(f) \nAn authorized delegate
          of a licensee holds in trust for the benefit of the \nlicensee all money
          net of fees received from money transmission.  If any authorized delegate
          \ncommingles any funds received from money transmission with any other funds
          or property owned \nor controlled by the authorized delegate, all commingled
          funds and other property shall be \nconsidered held in trust in favor of
          the licensee in an amount equal to the amount of money net of\n"

        available_excerpt: "31 \n \nfees received from money transmission.22 \n(g)
          \nAn authorized delegate may not use a subdelegate to conduct money \ntransmission
          on behalf of a licensee. \nSection 8.02 Unauthorized Activities \nA person
          shall not engage in the business of money transmission on behalf of a person
          \nnot licensed under this [Act]  or not exempt pursuant to [Article III]
          of this [Act]. A person that \nengages in such activity provides money transmission
          to the same extent as if the person were a \nlicensee, and shall be jointly
          and severally liable with the unlicensed or nonexempt person. \nSection
          8.03 [Optional]: Prohibited Authorized Delegates. \n(a) \nThe [appropriate
          court] in an action brought by a licensee shall have \njurisdiction to grant
          appropriate equitable or legal relief, including without limitation prohibiting
          \nthe authorized delegate from directly or indirectly acting as an authorized
          delegate for any licensee \nin this state and the payment of restitution,
          damages or other monetary relief, if the [appropriate \ncourt] finds that
          an authorized delegate failed to remit money in accordance with the written
          \ncontract required by [Section 8.01(b)] or as otherwise directed by the
          licensee or required by law. \n(b) \nIf the [appropriate court] issues an
          order prohibiting a person from acting as \nan authorized delegate for any
          licensee pursuant to [Section 8.03(a)], the licensee that brought the \naction
          shall report the order to the [Commissioner] within thirty (30) days and
          shall report the \norder through NMLS within ninety (90) days. \n(c) \nAn
          authorized delegate who holds money in trust for the benefit of a \nlicensee
          and knowingly fails to remit more than [$XXX] of such money is guilty of
          a [reference \nto state classification] felony. \n(d) \nAn authorized delegate
          who holds money in trust for the benefit of a \nlicensee and knowingly fails
          to remit no more than [$XXX] of such money is guilty of a [reference \nto
          state classification] misdemeanor. \nARTICLE IX  \nTimely Transmission,
          Refunds, and Disclosures \nSection 9.01 Timely Transmission. \n(a) \nEvery
          licensee shall forward all money received for transmission in \naccordance
          with the terms of the agreement between the licensee and the sender unless
          the licensee \nhas a reasonable belief or a reasonable basis to believe
          that the sender may be a victim of fraud or \nthat a crime or violation
          of law, rule, or regulation has occurred, is occurring, or may occur. \n(b)
          \nIf a licensee fails to forward money received for transmission in accordance
          \nwith this section, the licensee must respond to inquiries by the sender
          with the reason for the failure \n \n22 Commentary: An express trust account
          or segregated bank account is not required.\n"

        source_label: Money Transmitter Licensing | Department of Financial Services

        unit_id: s000001
        locator: Section 1, characters 2400–7324
        available_excerpt: 'ey Transmitter License.


          Access to NMLS


          NMLS is a secure web-based system created by state regulators to provide
          efficiencies in the processing of state licenses and improve supervision
          of state-regulated industries.


          To access NMLS for the first time, you must complete a Company Account Request
          Form and identify a Primary Account Administrator and a Secondary Account
          Administrator. This form can be submitted online through the NMLS website
          in the Getting Started section. This form needs to be submitted only once
          per company, regardless of the number of NMLS participating states in which
          you are licensed.


          Within three days of completing and submitting the Company Account Request
          Form, the Primary Account Administrator will receive NMLS login information.
          The Primary Account Administrator will have full rights to access the system,
          submit information to this agency and other participating state regulators,
          and set up other company users in the system. Instructions and tutorials
          on how to access and use the system are also available in the NMLS Resource
          Center .


          Note : If your company already has a record in NMLS, you can omit this step.


          Managing Your License on NMLS


          Each company holding a DFS Money Transmitter License who wishes to manage
          their license on NMLS must create a company record in the system. To gain
          access to NMLS, the applicant must submit a form requesting an NMLS account.


          Current New York State Money Transmitters may transition their licenses
          to NMLS. See the DFS Money Transmitter Transition Checklist for more information.


          Submitting a Complete Application


          To submit an application and ensure your application is received, acknowledged
          as complete, and processed, please follow the instructions on the DFS Money
          Transmitter Checklists . No application shall be deemed to be complete until
          the Department has received all required information, documents, and fees.


          In the process of reviewing and considering the application, DFS may request
          additional information and supporting documents.


          In the application process, an NMLS Identification Number will be assigned
          to your application. Please maintain a record of this NMLS Identification
          Number, as it will be used as your application reference number throughout
          the remainder of the application process. The applicant’s NMLS Identification
          Number must be included on every hard-copy document submitted to the Department.


          Note : If the applicant has already submitted Forms MU1 and MU2 through
          NMLS for another state, the applicant does not need to re-enter the company
          record into NMLS. However, the applicant is required to provide jurisdiction-specific
          information to support its New York State application.


          Back to Top ▲

          Annual Reporting


          The Annual Report should be prepared by qualified persons and submitted
          within 120 days following the close of the calendar year January 1 to December
          31, 2025.


          2025 NMLS Money Transmitter Annual Report Form


          2025 Non-NMLS Money Transmitter Annual Report Form


          Back to Top ▲


          Next Section


          Continue


          Reporting Change in Certain Individuals


          Pursuant to the following sections of the New York Banking Law (BL) and
          Superintendent’s Regulations (SR), licensees of the Department of Financial
          Services (DFS) are required to notify the Superintendent of changes in certain
          individuals, within stipulated time frames:


          Money Transmitters: BL 641, 642 and 652-a; and SR 406.11


          These requirements are for changes in certain individuals of licensees whose
          licenses are not managed on NMLS. For those managed on NMLS, visit the NMLS
          section website for New York State and navigate to Company Licenses and
          Amendment under the pertinent industry type, and look under Change in Control
          on the Amendment Checklist.


          Included Individuals


          Members of the governing board such as directors, trustees, and LLC members


          Officers (at a minimum Chief Executive Officer, President, Chief Financial
          Officer, Chief Compliance Officer, and Chief Operations Officer, and any
          other officers deemed necessary by DFS)


          Documentary requirements for Each Included Individual Being Added


          Notification on the licensee''s letterhead signed by an authorized officer
          containing the following:


          Name and title of the individual being added


          Effective date of the addition


          Name and title of the person being replaced, and his/her new title/position,
          if any


          Resolution of the governing board approving the addition


          Personal Questionnaire (PDF)


          Fingerprints


          Background Investigation Report *


          Litigation Affidavit (PDF)


          Authority to Release Information (PDF)


          Resume


          Documentary requirements for Each Included Individual Being Removed:


          Notification on the licensee''s letterhead signed by an authorized officer
          containing the following:


          Name and title of the individual being removed


          Reason of the removal


          Effective date of the removal


          New title/position, if any


          Where To Submit?'

        available_excerpt: 'How To Get A Money Transmitter License (MTL) in the U.S.


          Published Date  January 29, 2026


          To get a Money Transmitter License (MTL), businesses must undergo a rigorous
          application process that involves dual compliance with federal (like FinCEN''s
          AML/KYC protocols) and varying state-level regulations. Key requirements
          across states include demonstrating financial viability, often requiring
          a surety bond and capital reserves, passing comprehensive background checks
          for key personnel, and establishing a robust internal compliance program.
          The process is complex, time-consuming, and mandates extensive documentation
          and financial disclosures to ensure the applicant is law-abiding and financially
          sound.


          Operating a money transfer service in the U.S. involves tackling a myriad
          of federal and state laws, making how to get a money transmitter license
          both time-consuming and expensive. Compliance with agencies like FinCEN
          is non-negotiable to prevent illegal activities.


          Companies can either secure their own MSB license or partner with a licensed
          entity, but legal adherence is vital in both scenarios. It''s essential
          to understand what a money transmitter license is and who needs it.


          What is a Money Transmitter License?


          A Money Transmitter License is an official authorization or money service
          business license that empowers a firm or individual to facilitate the movement
          of capital. This license enables MSBs to handle financial transactions,
          ranging from digital payments to wire transfers.


          Possessing a Money Transmitter License brings forth substantial regulatory
          oversight. Organizations must prove they have the governance structure and
          internal controls to manage and safeguard client funds. States will continually
          scrutinize applicants, denying licensure to those who fail to meet the stringent
          criteria.


          In the United States, the need for a Money Transmitter License is not a
          choice; it''s a requirement for virtually any business involved in the handling
          or transferring of funds. Money transmitter license requirements by state
          can vary, so it''s crucial to be aware of the respective state money transmitter
          regulations.


          How to Get a Money Transmitter License?


          The license application process is designed to be rigorous, ensuring that
          approved businesses are law-abiding and financially sound. Federal and state-level
          regulations diverge, with each state setting its own financial criteria
          and often requiring a minimum capital commitment.


          Applicants typically need a surety bond of at least $500,000 per state,
          with costs influenced by credit history. The duration to obtain the license
          varies, contingent on the business type and the state of operation.


          Money Transmitter License Requirements


          Acquiring a money transmitter license involves compliance with Anti-Money
          Laundering (AML) and Know Your Customer (KYC) protocols. While these regulations
          are federal, individual states often impose additional requirements, thereby
          necessitating dual compliance.


          Subsequent to application submission, state authorities undertake an investigative
          review, focusing on financial sustainability and the applicant''s background.


          Standardized Requirements Across States


          Registration: Initial registration typically occurs with the Financial Crimes
          Enforcement Network or a similar state-level body.'

        url: https://www.troutmanfinancialservices.com/2026/06/occ-confirms-national-bank-act-preempts-state-money-transmitter-licensing-for-fidelity-digital-assets/

        path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413/e06621859d4ec9431f2712a7c357b112/sections/s000001.md
        source_hash: 8ef30c0b98621db1f11c16332c16e9928ea8f237d6b055f645f7b449f18cbdfb
        source_label: OCC Confirms National Bank Act Preempts State Money Transmitter
          ... — Section 1, characters 600–4794
        unit_id: s000001
        locator: Section 1, characters 600–4794
        available_excerpt: ', 2026


          Posted in Bank Regulatory


          On May 12, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued a
          significant interpretive letter confirming that Fidelity Digital Assets,
          National Association (the recently converted national trust bank formerly
          known as Fidelity Digital Assets Service, LLC) is not required to hold state
          money transmitter licenses to conduct its federally authorized activities.
          The OCC concluded that the National Bank Act preempts any state money transmitter
          licensing requirement as applied to a national bank.


          Until December 12, 2025, Fidelity Digital Assets operated as a New York-chartered
          limited liability trust company and held money transmitter licenses in numerous
          states, including Iowa. On that date, the OCC approved its conversion to
          an uninsured national trust bank under 12 U.S.C. § 27(a). Concurrent with
          the conversion, the Bank surrendered its Iowa money transmitter license.


          Iowa pushed back. Its money transmitter statute exempts banks and trust
          companies from licensing, but only if they hold federally insured deposits.
          Because Fidelity Digital Assets is an uninsured national bank, Iowa argued
          the exemption did not apply and requested a legal basis for the license
          surrender. Fidelity Digital Assets responded that the National Bank Act
          preempts Iowa’s requirements and asked the OCC to confirm that position.


          The OCC’s analysis of whether a state can require a national bank to obtain
          a state money transmitter license as a condition of engaging in federally
          authorized activities, including cryptocurrency custody, trade execution,
          stablecoin issuance, and related digital asset services, rested on two independent
          and well-established pillars of federal banking law:


          1. National Bank Act Preemption


          Federal law authorizes national banks to conduct a broad range of activities
          on a national basis. Any state law that “prevents or significantly interferes”
          with a national bank’s exercise of its federally authorized powers is preempted.


          The OCC reasoned that requiring a national bank to obtain a state money
          transmitter license, even as a threshold condition to operating, would impermissibly
          condition the Bank’s federal authority on state approval. At the extreme,
          a state could veto federal authority outright by denying or revoking a license.
          Both outcomes are squarely preempted. This conclusion applies to any state’s
          money transmitter licensing regime, including states that limit their licensing
          exemptions to a subset of national banks (such as Iowa’s insured-deposits-only
          carveout).


          2. Exclusive Federal Visitorial Authority


          Separately, 12 U.S.C. § 484 vests the OCC with exclusive visitorial authority
          over national banks. “No national bank shall be subject to any visitorial
          powers except as authorized by Federal law.” Iowa’s money transmitter statute
          grants the state agency robust supervisory jurisdiction over licensees,
          including the power to demand books and records, conduct periodic examinations,
          take enforcement actions, and even place a licensee into receivership. Applying
          that regime to a national bank would be “fundamentally inconsistent” with
          the OCC’s exclusive visitorial powers and is therefore impermissible on
          independent grounds.


          Together, these two bases lead to a clean and sweeping conclusion: a national
          bank may conduct its federally authorized activities in any state without
          a state money transmitter license, regardless of whether it qualifies for
          any state-law exemption.


          Our Take


          The OCC’s conclusion here was entirely expected. The preemption framework
          for national banks is well-settled, and the OCC’s letter largely restates
          principles the Supreme Court and federal courts have applied for decades.
          That said, one nuance in this letter deserves closer attention: state-chartered
          trust banks are in a very different position.


          Unlike national banks, state trust companies and state-chartered banks do
          not benefit from National Bank Act preemption. Their ability to avoid state
          money transmitter licensing requirements depends entirely on how each individual
          state defines “bank” or “trust company” in its money transmission statute
          and those definitions vary considerably.

# Harbor 2 — Harbor Pay acquisition migration: pre-close legal review

## Current position

**Yes — several parts of the migration need legal review before the Nov 15 close, and at least two of them determine what the day-1 migration can actually cover.** Dana (PM, Growth & Integration) asked on 2026-09-09 whether anything in the Harbor Pay plan "need[s] legal," presenting it as essentially a data migration. The record supports a different answer: the plan moves 252k customers (240k consumer + 12k business) into Mosaic Relay's app on day 1, without re-verification, onto Mosaic's license and monitoring infrastructure, plus a new $50 bonus — a regulated transition with a short clock.

The two scope-changing items are:

- **State licensing.** The intake answer says Mosaic plans to "use/assume Harbor's licenses" for the new markets opened by the combined footprint (2026-09-09). On an asset purchase, licenses are entity-specific and generally do not transfer by operation of law; states commonly require approval, notice, or a new application. Until verified state by state, the migration should be limited to states where Mosaic's licenses are current, with the Harbor-only states phased or deferred.
- **KYC.** "No re-verification" depends on compliance confirming whether Mosaic's AML/CIP program permits reliance on Harbor's prior KYC — recorded as "not sure / need to check with compliance" — and on what happens to pre-2023 users whose underlying documents are gone.

The most decision-changing item is the **unread alerts and SARs** (~40 open alerts, "a handful" of SARs, never reviewed): findings can affect the deal itself, and the review must run under a controlled handling protocol because SAR disclosure is restricted (Issue 5).

**Recommended course (this draft).** Keep Nov 15 as the deal milestone, but make legal/compliance readiness a gate on migration scope, not on the close. Start now on: (1) license verification and state transferability analysis; (2) the alert/SAR handling protocol and review; (3) the written KYC-reliance determination plus a pre-2023 cohort plan; (4) a validated monitoring cutover plan with a parallel run before close; (5) bonus-term clearance. The technical/data build, the reviews themselves, and migration within Mosaic's licensed footprint for resolved cohorts can proceed in parallel. What should wait: go-live in the Harbor-only states, migration of unresolved cohorts, the close+1 bonus campaign, and any reading of SARs outside the protocol. Phasing the launch solves the licensing-timeline mismatch; it does not solve KYC, monitoring, or alert review, and it does not clear the earlier milestone — migrating only within Mosaic's states still depends on those conditions.

**Status of the view.** The saved records already treat legal and compliance readiness as a pre-close gate and warn against assuming license transfer (2026-09-10 22:49 status summary, submitted on the scenario path but addressing the matter, which also lists a narrower launch as the fallback if licensing, KYC records, alert review, or monitoring tests are incomplete). No recorded decision in the material read adopts a course, and generating this dossier records none. A 2026-09-10 04:36 tracked dossier revision (adds options, a working recommendation, material unknowns, source limits) is proposed, not accepted. This draft's additions are the phased-launch recommendation, the SAR-handling protocol, and the customer data/consent review.

## Decision question

Does any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration need legal review before the Nov 15 close?

## Issues

Support status, stated once: the material read for this draft contains no retrieved external authority; the research run started 2026-09-10 is not shown as delivered in the material read. Authorities below are named as leads and flagged **Needs checking**; the analysis is conditional on them. No saved issue IDs appeared in the material read, so issues are identified by heading.

### Issue 1 — Licensing: serving the Harbor-only markets after an asset purchase

**Current answer.** Mosaic should not plan on operating under Harbor's MTLs in the new markets at close. Money transmitter licensure is state-specific and entity-specific; an asset purchase does not transfer Harbor's licenses, and each state decides whether the transaction needs prior approval, notice, a new license, or nothing at all. Because Mosaic would be the entity serving the migrated customers, Mosaic needs its own authority (or a recognized transfer/approval) for each state at issue. Interim course: scope day-1 migration to states where Mosaic's licenses are verified and current, and phase the Harbor-only states pending approvals — state timelines are likely to exceed the time to Nov 15. Note that the size of the problem is itself unverified: the reported counts are internally inconsistent (see Record conflicts).

**Rule and support.** State money transmitter statutes govern licensing and change-of-control/transfer approval; the requirement and process vary by state. Examples to verify: California Money Transmission Act (Cal. Fin. Code § 2000 et seq.), New York money transmitter licensing (N.Y. Banking Law § 640 et seq.; 3 NYCRR Part 417), Texas Money Services Act (Tex. Fin. Code ch. 152), and the Money Transmission Modernization Act as adopted in various states — all **Needs checking**. Federal registration is also entity-specific (31 C.F.R. § 1022.380, MSB registration) **Needs checking**. No retrieved authority is saved in the material read.

**Application.** Mosaic becomes the service provider to 252k consumers and businesses; money transmission to customers in a state generally requires licensure in that state. On an asset purchase, Harbor's licenses remain Harbor's; many states review changes of control or asset transfers and some prohibit operation under a transferred license without approval. Consequence: if approvals cannot be obtained pre-close, either those customers are excluded from the day-1 migration or they remain on Harbor's platform after close (which depends on deal and servicing arrangements not established in the record). A phased launch addresses the licensing gap only; it leaves KYC (Issue 2) and monitoring (Issue 3) as independent gates.

**Next step.** Deliverable: jurisdiction-level license schedules for both companies (NMLS and state regulator records) plus per-state advice on transfer, approval, or new application and expected timelines. Result needed: which states Mosaic can lawfully serve at close. Dependent: the day-1 launch-scope decision. Fallback: phased launch; defer the Harbor-only states; do not rely on "assume Harbor's licenses." This is the most time-sensitive item because state review can be slower than the remaining runway.

### Issue 2 — KYC: migration without re-verification and the pre-2023 records

**Current answer.** Unresolved and fact-dependent. Whether the 252k users can migrate without re-verification is unknown because compliance has not confirmed whether Mosaic's own AML/CIP program permits reliance on Harbor's prior KYC (recorded intake answer: "not sure / need to check with compliance"). Separately, the missing underlying documents for users onboarded before 2023 are not cured by pass/fail results if Mosaic's program or its examiners expect the records; plan a risk-based path for that cohort (re-verify, step-up, or limit products) if the documents cannot be reconstructed. Do not migrate an unresolved cohort until the written determination lands.

**Rule and support.** Bank Secrecy Act, 31 U.S.C. § 5311 et seq.; MSB AML program requirements, 31 C.F.R. § 1022.210; SAR rule, 31 C.F.R. § 1022.320; recordkeeping rules, 31 C.F.R. §§ 1010.311, 1010.410 — **Needs checking**. Express federal reliance on another institution's CIP performance exists for banks (31 C.F.R. § 1020.220(a)(6)) **Needs checking**; do not assume the same path applies to a money transmitter — whether it does, and on what conditions, is the research question. Mosaic's own AML/CIP program is a private standard and the immediate constraint here. Also confirm whether customer due diligence or beneficial-ownership expectations apply to the 12k business accounts as Mosaic will hold them **Needs checking**.

**Application.** If reliance is confirmed and the program is satisfied, the migration can proceed as planned. If not, re-verification or cohort-level treatment is required. The likely middle case: reliance confirmed as a policy matter, but documentation expectations and examiner practice still create risk for the pre-2023 cohort, mitigated by a targeted refresh. Unresolved cohort treatment changes the day-1 customer set, not just internal process. The migration also creates new account and transaction records after close; responsibility for those should be explicit in the integration plan.

**Next step.** Deliverable: written compliance determination on reliance plus a pre-2023 cohort plan (method, cost, timing). Result needed: migrate as-is versus re-verify/limit. Dependent: day-1 cohort composition. Fallback: exclude or step-up the pre-2023 cohort and cover legacy recordkeeping with deal protections. This is the work already assigned to compliance in the intake record ("need to check with compliance").

### Issue 3 — Alerts, SAR history, and transaction-monitoring continuity at close

**Current answer.** This is the highest-risk item and a pre-close one. The ~40 unread open alerts and the unreviewed SARs from the last year mean Harbor's suspicious-activity pipeline is unresolved; the findings can affect the deal (price, conditions, indemnities) and post-close obligations. They should be reviewed before close — but only through the controlled protocol in Issue 5. On monitoring: Harbor's third-party monitoring contract terminates at close and the plan is a day-1 repoint of the feed to Mosaic's engine; without validation, a cutover gap means undetected activity and missed filings. Run a parallel test with pass criteria before close, with a fallback of dual-running or manual review until validated. Do not treat the repoint as a data-plumbing item.

**Rule and support.** MSB AML programs must include detection and reporting of suspicious activity (31 C.F.R. § 1022.210) and SARs must be filed (§ 1022.320); SAR confidentiality is statutory (31 U.S.C. § 5318(g)(2)) — **Needs checking**. Effective monitoring is a program requirement; the parallel run is a recommended risk control to meet it, not itself a legal rule. Filing duties are entity-specific: Harbor files for pre-close activity it detects; Mosaic files for post-close activity it detects. Allocate these responsibilities in the deal documents. No retrieved authority is saved in the material read.

**Application.** Unreviewed alerts are unresolved reportable-activity questions; if anything is reportable and unfiled, the fix is time-sensitive (Harbor filing before or around close, or a documented post-close process). Alert review also provides information about the migrated customer base that should feed Mosaic's post-close risk assessment. The monitoring cutover determines whether post-close activity is detected at all — these two items are linked: the backlog concerns what was already missed, the cutover concerns what happens next. Either can change the go/no-go for the day-1 migration.

**Next step.** Deliverables: (a) the controlled review protocol and findings summary (Issue 5); (b) a cutover test plan with pass/fail criteria and a defined fallback. Result needed: whether findings change the deal, and whether the repoint is safe. Dependent: close terms and day-1 migration scope. Fallback: closing conditions and indemnity if the review is incomplete; dual-run or manual review if testing fails.

### Issue 4 — The $50 welcome bonus (close+1 campaign)

**Current answer.** Not a deal blocker, but review before launch. The material read has no campaign terms. The review should cover eligibility ("first transfer" — from what, by when), how the credit is delivered (does it land in the unified balance), disclosures, and any state advertising requirements that apply to licensed transmitters. Launch states should align with the licensed footprint from Issue 1; a campaign aimed at customers Mosaic cannot yet lawfully serve would compound the licensing problem.

**Rule and support.** Federal unfairness and deception standards: FTC Act § 5 (15 U.S.C. § 45); CFPB UDAAP (12 U.S.C. §§ 5531, 5536) — **Needs checking** (applicability to this offer and entity unverified). State money transmitter advertising and marketing provisions and state UDAP statutes — **Needs checking**. No retrieved authority is saved in the material read.

**Application.** If the terms are clear and disclosures accurate, residual risk is low. Recurring risk points: ambiguity about what qualifies as a "first transfer," bonus availability windows, and how a promotional credit is treated relative to customer funds (relevant if it interacts with the unified balance or safeguarding). The close+1 timing adds little legal pressure — the campaign can be delayed without affecting the close or the migration.

**Next step.** Deliverable: reviewed campaign terms and disclosures. Result needed: launch clearance. Dependent: the close+1 campaign. Fallback: hold the campaign until cleared. Proposed owner: marketing with compliance review; timing is tied to close+1, not to close itself.

### Issue 5 — Handling SARs and alert records in diligence (newly identified in this draft; no saved issue ID)

**Current answer.** Put a controlled access and handling protocol in place before the SARs are read. SAR disclosure is restricted by law, and SARs should not be transferred to Mosaic's deal team pre-close without a legal basis. Practical path: Harbor — its BSA officer and counsel — performs the review; Mosaic receives only what may permissibly be shared, in a form sufficient for deal decisions; the protocol governs what goes into the data room and the deal documents. This is the sequencing gate for Issue 3. Source and effect: the diligence facts (unread alerts and SARs; "nothing reviewed yet") plus the plan to review them in diligence — if the protocol is wrong, either the review stalls or the confidentiality restriction is breached.

**Rule and support.** 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g)(2) and the implementing MSB rule, 31 C.F.R. § 1022.320, restrict disclosure of SARs; the permissible scope of sharing with a prospective buyer or its counsel, and any exceptions, are unverified — **Needs checking**. Distinguish permitted diligence review from disclosure or transfer of the restricted material; a request to assess exposure is not an instruction to hand over SARs.

**Application.** Done correctly, the review can still inform closing conditions, indemnities, and integration planning through permitted channels, and Mosaic's post-close filing regime can be planned with knowledge of the backlog. Done incorrectly, the deal risks a confidentiality violation and loss of the review's usefulness. Mosaic does not "inherit" Harbor's SARs or their filing duties as such — its obligations attach to activity it detects as the operating entity.

**Next step.** Deliverable: written protocol — who may access, where, how documented, what Mosaic may receive and in what form. Result needed: permitted, usable findings. Dependent: the Issue 3 review. Fallback: if the protocol cannot be agreed before close, protect the deal with closing conditions and indemnities and complete the review promptly post-close with Harbor's cooperation. Proposed owner: Harbor BSA officer with outside counsel; Mosaic receives filtered output.

### Issue 6 — Day-1 customer and data migration: consent, privacy, and contract assignment (newly identified in this draft; no saved issue ID)

**Current answer.** Review before close. Three strands: (a) Harbor's customer agreements — whether they permit assignment or transfer, and what notice or consent is required before accounts move; (b) privacy — which federal and state privacy rules govern moving and using 252k customers' data, including any limits on sharing with Mosaic and required notices; (c) the "one unified account, one balance" model — document whose balance it is and where the funds sit, because that funds-flow description also drives the licensing analysis and the bank-holds-funds alternative. None of this appears reviewed in the material read. Source and effect: the migration plan itself (accounts and data into Mosaic's app with full product access) — these items condition the migration mechanics.

**Rule and support.** GLBA privacy provisions, 15 U.S.C. §§ 6801–6809, and implementing rules as applicable to the entities involved (e.g., 12 C.F.R. Part 1016 for some financial institutions; regulator-specific rules for others) — **Needs checking**; state privacy statutes and state UDAP — **Needs checking**. Contract assignment and novation are governed by Harbor's customer terms and general contract principles; those terms are private agreements, not public law. No retrieved authority is saved in the material read.

**Application.** An asset purchase does not automatically carry customer contracts or consent to data use. If the agreements require notice or consent, moving customers first creates contract and unfairness exposure and state regulator attention. Privacy notices may need updating before the move. The unified-balance description is a prerequisite for assessing both the licensing question and the bank alternative — a change in who holds funds does not by itself remove a permission requirement; the answer follows the actual funds flow and customer relationship.

**Next step.** Deliverable: a data map, a notice/consent determination, the assignment analysis, and a funds-flow description for the unified balance. Dependent: migration mechanics and launch scope. Fallback: stage the data move or hold specific features (such as the unified balance) until consents and notices are in place. Proposed owner: privacy counsel with Dana.

## Next actions

Nov 15 is a recorded business target from the request, not a legal deadline in the material read. Suggested owners are marked **Proposed** unless the record already assigns the work.

1. **License verification and state transferability analysis** — Deliverable: jurisdiction-level license schedules plus per-state requirements and timelines for the Harbor-only states. ## Alternatives considered

### Alternative: a partner bank holds the funds

**Hypothetical — not adopted.** Raised by the lawyer on 2026-09-10 (23:03, repeated 23:35) and analyzed on the scenario path; the record states the current matter position stays unchanged, and no external authority was retrieved for the hypothetical.

Assumptions, kept hypothetical: a partner bank holds customer funds while Mosaic supplies technology and operations.

**Benefits.** This could lower licensing risk if the bank owns the accounts and controls fund transfers (the record's analysis). That is the only benefit established in the saved material; it is unverified and depends on the bank actually holding the relationship and the transfers.

**Trade-offs and added risks.** It does not automatically remove risk if Mosaic controls transfers, owes balances, or acts directly for users (record). More generally, changing the actor or channel does not itself remove a permission requirement — the licensing answer follows the actual funds flow and customer relationship, which the record does not map. Feasibility also depends on bank terms and arrangements not present in the material read, so the alternative cannot be treated as available until that work is done.

**Issues that remain.** KYC reliance, the pre-2023 records, alerts/SARs, monitoring continuity, and the marketing/bonus questions all remain unchanged (record). The alternative does not resolve any of them, though the SAR-handling protocol and the data/consent review (Issues 5 and 6) would still be needed.

**Next action and comparison.** Recorded next step: map the funds flow, customer relationship, and compliance duties before assessing this option. Recommendation for sequencing: keep the current direction — direct migration into Mosaic's app — as the baseline with a phased launch, because it is the planned path and the alternative's licensing benefit is unverified and would require funds-flow and contract work that has not started. Revisit the bank model only if the licensing analysis (action 1) shows Mosaic cannot reach the Harbor-only markets in time and the bank structure is genuinely available; if used, it would change the funds-holding layer, not the KYC, monitoring, alert, or marketing gates, which would still apply.

## Record conflicts

**License counts versus "four new markets."** The request reports Harbor holding MTLs in 38 states, Mosaic in 41, a combined 44, opening "four new markets." The arithmetic is inconsistent with that conclusion: a combined footprint of 44 with Mosaic at 41 implies three Harbor-only states, not four; four new markets would require a combined 45 or different underlying counts. Effect: the number of states requiring transfer approval or new licensing — the core licensing scope — is uncertain, and the launch-scope decision depends on it. Resolution: jurisdiction-level license lists from NMLS or state regulator records for both companies.

**Metadata date versus reported milestones.** The matter record lists a target date of 2026-09-11, which matches no reported milestone in the material read (the reported milestones are the Nov 15 close, the day-1 migration, and the close+1 campaign). No effect on the analysis is established; confirm what that date represents before relying on it.

## Assumptions used

1. Mosaic's reported 41-state license footprint is current and sufficient for the states where it will continue serving customers at close. The phased-launch recommendation depends on this; verify against license records.
2. The pre-2023 cohort can be identified and either excluded or step-up-verified operationally. The KYC fallback depends on this; if not, whole-cohort treatment changes.
3. A parallel-run monitoring test is feasible before close, with access to Harbor's feed and a test environment. The no-gap recommendation depends on this; otherwise use dual-running or manual review plus closing conditions.
4. Harbor can and will run the alert/SAR review pre-close and provide only permitted, filtered output to Mosaic. Issues 3 and 5 and action 2 depend on this; if not, deal protections carry more weight.
5. The deal documentation can still accommodate closing conditions, representations, and indemnities at this stage. The fallbacks in Issues 2, 3, and 5 and action 8 depend on this.
